Ethics Committee (IEC) at each participating site. A list of all IRBs/IECs used in this study is provided

5.2. 
Ethical Conduct of the Study 
The study was conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) as required by the 
International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) guidelines and the FDA. Compliance with these 
requirements also constitutes conformity with the US 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 50 
(Protection of Human Subjects), US 21 Part 56 (Institutional Review Boards), ICH Harmonised 
Tripartite Guideline, Guideline for GCP E6(R1), the Nuremburg Code, and the ethical principles of the 
Declaration of Helsinki. 
5.3. 
Subject Information and Consent 
Copies of the IRB-approved Informed Consent Form (ICF) were received and reviewed by Histogenics 
Corporation (Sponsor) prior to the enrollment of patients at an investigational site. The ICF document 
approved by the site’s IRB was signed by the patient and the Investigator prior to enrollment. The 
Investigator provided a copy of the signed ICF to the patient, and the original was retained by the 
Investigator. A sample ICF is provided in Section 16.1.3.2.

7. 
INTRODUCTION 
Cartilage is the specialized fibrous connective tissue of primarily mesenchymal origin that forms the 
skeleton of the human body during development that is replaced with bone. Mature cartilage forming 
cells (chondrocytes) secrete the components of the extracellular matrix (hyaluronan, chondroitin sulfates 
and keratan sulfate) and tropocollagen, which polymerizes extracellularly into fine collagen fibers. 
Cartilage persists in the growing fetus, throughout development and into adulthood in further 
differentiated forms. The three most common are articular hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage. Articular 
cartilage is hyaline cartilage that covers the surface of bones at the joint space acting as a shock absorber 
and enabling the bones to glide over each other with minimal friction. Articular cartilage is covered by 
the synovial membrane which secretes the non-Newtonian synovial fluid that keeps the joint lubricated. 
Damage to the articular cartilage may be due to acute injury or repetitive trauma, and patients often 
experience pain and loss of function for several years due to the lack of efficacious medical treatments. 
The existence of a cartilage defect in the knee joint is an important clinical finding since full thickness 
defects do not heal spontaneously once skeletal maturity is reached (Chalmers, 2013) and can result in 
debilitating symptoms such as pain, swelling, catching and grinding with knee movement (Bhosale and 
Richardson, 2008). Although chondrocytes produce matrix components throughout life, their production 
is unable to keep pace with the repair requirements after acute damage to hyaline cartilage. If cartilage is 
injured after a period of active growth, the defects are usually filled by connective tissue or fibrous 
cartilage. The extracellular matrix of these repair tissues is only poorly integrated with the matrix of the 
damaged cartilage. In addition, these types of repair tissue have less resiliency than mature articular 
cartilage. Left untreated, such lesions may progress to degenerative osteoarthritis (Buckwalter and 
Mankin, 1998), which is the third leading cause of work disability in adult populations in the United 
States (Theis et al., 2017). By extension, disability and the often-associated opioid addiction crisis is an 
enormous contributor to the annual pharmacoeconomic burden and medical costs to society. The 
ultimate goal of treatment of cartilage injuries in the knee is for clinicians to be able to restore joint 
function to pre-injury levels in a timely, predictable and durable fashion. 
There is a significant unmet medical need for knee cartilage defects resulting in symptoms of pain and 
reduced function. Although treatment options for cartilage defects in the knee have evolved over the past 
25 years, there remains a need for predictable and durable treatments. With current surgical strategies, 
many patients remain symptomatic, or symptoms return within one to two years of the intervention. In 
the United States, based on reimbursement codes demonstrating incidence, it is believed that 
approximately 1.2 million patients each year have arthroscopies where focal cartilage defects are 
identified. Only approximately 500,000 patients ultimately receive treatment with the large majority 
being debridement and microfracture (Mfx). Despite the limitations of microfracture, there are still 
approximately 150,000 microfracture procedures done each year. 
Due to the variable outcomes of current treatment options including the prolonged rehabilitation phase, 
many patients elect to tolerate knee pain and loss of function with as many as   60% of patients avoiding 
or delaying treatment. These cartilage injuries, along with other knee injuries, are believed to be one of 
the primary predictors of later stage osteoarthritis. These injuries can have a significant economic impact 
for both the patient and the health care system with time lost from work, progression of disease and 
potential eventual need for joint replacement. Better treatment options are particularly important given 
the youngerdemographics of the affected individuals in their prime earning, sporting, or childraising 
years.

Clinical trials in the cartilage treatment space have been challenging to conduct due to patient 
perceptions regarding microfracture, difficult to recruit due to the specific inclusion / exclusion criteria 
for isolated defects, and until recent FDA guidance, lacked clarity on the appropriate endpoints for 
evaluation in clinical studies. Due to the paucity of adequate and well-controlled clinical studies in the 
United States, it is also difficult to make meaningful comparisons across treatment modalities. 
The current treatment options can be broadly classified into three categories and are described in Table 
2. Palliation (chondroplasty and debridement), repair (microfracture) or restorative (mosaicplasty, 
osteochondral auto or allograft, autologous chondrocyte implantation). While all have demonstrated 
benefit, especially in specific patient populations, there are many limitations and clinicans and patients 
have sought a better solution across the range of lesion sizes and body types.

7.1. 
Repairative Treatments 
While chondroplasty and debridement can alleviate pain for some period of time by trimming and 
smoothing damaged cartilage in the knee, they are not curative procedures.  The area of damaged 
cartilage is unable to regenerate and create a smooth hyaline covered joint.  This limitation is what led

Page 16 of 138 
 
CLINICAL STUDY REPORT 
attempts to either allow the body to self repair the defect or provide the necessary cells to replace the 
missing cartilage and integrate into the patient’s native knee cartilage.  These methods have been met 
with varying degrees of success. While all of the treatment options are perceived as less than ideal, 
industry and the FDA sought to determine the most appropriate control arm for clinical development.  
Debridement does not treat the underlying defect, and auto/allograft tissue results are variable and not 
consistently available.   Microfracture had become the standard of care starting approximately 20 years 
ago, particularly for smaller lesions, and protocols were developed to provide for a fair basis of 
comparison to this repair procedure. 
7.2. 
Microfracture 
In 1997, Steadman, et al., introduced the concept of “microfracture” as a reparative approach to chondral 
defects [8]. As originally performed, the focal defect is debrided until the subchondral bone plate is 
visualized. Using an arthroscopic awl, a series of holes 3-4 mm apart are created (with 3 to 4 holes/cm2) 
such that bone marrow is released to create a fibrin clot filled with endogenous reparative-stimulating 
agents (e.g., mesenchymal stem cells, growth factors, and cell-signaling proteins).  Mesenchymal stem 
cells within the clot begin to proliferate, and several weeks after the procedure, cell differentiation 
creates cells that histologically appear similar to cartilage progenitor cells [9]. As time elapses (in terms 
of months and years), fibrocartilage – not hyaline cartilage – comprises most of the former defect. 
During the initial post-procedure timeframe, the clot may become dislodged leading to early failure.  To 
prevent this, patients must be non-weightbearing for a minimum of 6 weeks and then slowly progress to 
increased activity over the next 6 to 8 months with high impact activities and sports initiated after the 1-
year mark.  This Steadman defined rehabilitation protocol is deemed to be critically important - this 
slow progression and the strict adherence to a rehabilitation protocol is essential for success of the 
procedure and yet in reality can be difficult for patients to maintain given the normal demands of work 
and life.  Such rehabilitation protocol was utilized in the NeoCart Phase III trial to ensure best possible 
outcomes with microfracture. 
Unfortunately, even when proper rehabilitation is followed the clot may not heal or it may heal with soft 
fibrocartilage that lacks the resilience of articular cartilage.  This accounts for the high failure rate often 
seen with microfracture starting 2 to 4 years after treatment and recent literature suggests that the failure 
rate at 5 years may be as high as 60%, with the median time of failure being at 4 years (Solheim, 2018).   
Over the last 20 years, clinicans now recognize, however, that the quality of clinical outcomes after 
microfracture is dependent upon several variables.  Proper patient selection, surgical technique, and 
regimented physical therapy/rehabilitation all affect clinical outcome and patient satisfaction; each of 
these factors are addressed below. 
7.2.1. 
Patient selection and success factors 
Mithoefer, et al., [10] conducted a meta-analysis to systematically examine the clinical efficacy 
of microfracture by identifying studies that featured short- and long-term functional outcome scores, 
macroscopic and microscopic cartilage repair quality, and results from postoperative MRI assessments.  
The researchers identified 28 studies describing 3122 patients. By integrating the results of these studies, 
the authors identified a series of factors that affect the clinical outcome after microfracture.  Their table 
[10] is reproduced below (Table 3).

As seen above, assiduous patient selection is key to achieving positive outcomes after microfracture 
surgery. The researchers found, similar to the findings of Kreuz, et al. [11], that patients over 40 years of 
age tended to have worse outcomes than their younger counterparts.  Lesions smaller than 4 cm2 were 
associated with better outcomes; the study by Kreuz, et al. [11] indicated that defects >2 cm2 tended to 
have worse outcomes, thus tightening their criteria for optimal patients. In this regard, a meta-analysis of 
Goyal, et al. [12] agrees with both groups of previously cited researchers: in their study, good clinical 
outcomes were associated with small lesions in younger patients with low post-operative demands. 
In a 2016 review paper, Sommerfeldt, et al. [13], describe characteristics of a patient most likely to 
benefit from the microfracture procedure, “it [microfracture] is more likely to be successful when 
performed as a primary procedure for nonobese patients under the age of thirty to forty years with small 
(<2 to 4-cm2) femoral condylar defects that have been symptomatic for a short time (less than twelve to 
twenty-four months).” 
7.2.2. 
Microfracture Surgical Technique 
The underlying principle of microfracture is to access the pluripotent mesenchymal stem cells present in 
bone marrow – found just under subchondral bone – in order to stimulate the repair of cartilage defects. 
The goal, then, is to optimize the availability of these reparative cells within the defect. The techniques 
developed to achieve this goal are immensely varied: hole spacing (density), hole depth, method of hole 
creation (awls vs. drills), whether or not to create holes (and risk structural damage to subchondral 
bone). Chen, et al. [14], examined the creation of holes via compaction (i.e., micro-“fracture” via awls) 
vs. water-cooled drilling and the role of hole depth. Four micro-holes were created in the trochlear 
groove of New Zealand white rabbits: 1 hole ~2 mm in depth was created using an awl, 2 holes created 
by a drill to a depth of ~2 mm and the remaining hole drilled to a depth of ~6 mm; these series of 4 holes 
were replicated bilaterally in a total of 2 rabbits. The rabbits were sacrificed at 24 hours and the 
subchondral surfaces were examined histologically.  The authors found that the compaction of bone 
using an awl created channels with restricted blood egress due residual bony remnants.  The drilled 
channels were free of bony remnants and provided patent holes for blood egress.  The authors had 
expected to find that drilling would create thermal necrosis in nearby osteocytes, but this did not occur. 
Surprisingly, they found disruption of nearby osteophytes during compaction, which they attributed to 
high shear forces created during the microfracture process. They concluded that the creation of 
microchannels via drilling was preferred over the use of awls in order to create patent holes that would 
encourage the flow of pluripotent cells. 
While microfracture technique likely influences functional outcomes, a study by Kroell, et al. [15] 
demonstrates the difficulty in achieving uniformity of technique.  In their research, the authors instruct 
four surgeons to create microfracture holes of a prescribed depth and density (i.e., spacing) in six pre-

prepared chondral defects in fresh cadaveric knees.  They observed, “all surgeons misjudged depth and 
inter-hole distance tending to make microfracture holes too deep (depth error 1.1 mm + 1.9) and too 
close together (inter-hole distance error: -0.8 mm + 0.4).”  The authors concluded, “even experienced 
knee arthroscopy surgeons demonstrate inconsistency in surgical technique when performing 
microfracture.”  
7.3. 
Restoration (Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation) 
7.3.1. 
Carticel (Genzyme Corporation, now Vericel, Inc.) 
Articular cartilage cannot repair itself and microfracture, while widespread in adoption, has significant 
limitations. In an effort to provide a true cartilage repair option, Genzyme Corporation developed the 
technique of harvesting a biopsy of a patient’s own healthy cartilage and amplifying the cells through 
ex-vivo culture before placing the cells back into the patient and securing them in the defect with a 
patient-harvested periostal patch to promote integration. Carticel was originally available in 1995 as an 
unregulated therapy as the cells came from the patient’s own body. The FDA was in the process of 
implementing a new policy for biologics that was released in February 1997 and convened an advisory 
panel.  The panel voted 11-0 with one abstention that Carticel provided a clinical benefit to patient with 
damage to the articular cartilage of the knee. Carticel recieved accelerated approval from the FDA in 
August of 1997 after the FDA instituted specific cell therapy guidelines.  Under accelerated approval, 
the FDA required Genzyme to conduct confirmatory post-marketing studies which it completed in 2007, 
after which it approved new labeling that incorporated the safety and efficacy data from the STAR trial.  
There have now been several published reports of long term results following ACI.  The surgical 
procedure was described by Petersen et al. YEAR? showing functional improvement at 2 years and 
further improvement at long term follow-up between 5 and 11 years following implantation for 44 
patients with osteochondritis dissecans or with defects on the femoral condyle alone or with anterior 
cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction.  The modified Cincinnati Knee Score was significantly higher 
both at 2 years and at long term follow-up when compared to the baseline score.  There was an increase 
in the Knee Score from 2 years and long term follow-up, but the significance of this increase was not 
discussed.  Of note, there were 10 treatment failures (16%) of the 61 patients enrolled.  Earlier data from 
what is believed to be part of the same group of patients was presented by Petersen et al. YEAR? These 
earlier data showed that the modified Cincinnati Knee Scores were statistically improved at baseline 
compared with the post-operative scores.  These results are consistent with the later findings.19  
Henderson et al. YEAR? described two series of consecutive patients treated with ACI who were 
followed for 12 and 24 months, respectively.  There was a reduction in the Objective International Knee 
Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores in both groups at 3 months that essentially returned to 
baseline by 12 months.  There was no statistical difference between the 12 and 24 month scores.  The 
Subjective Knee Score was significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and this trend continued at 
24 months, but the increase was not significant.  Similarly, the ICRS Functional Knee Status was 
significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and even a bit higher at 24 months, but again, the 24 
month Functional Knee Status was not significantly different than the 12 month scores.21, .  The 
Subjective Knee Score was significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and this trend continued at 
24 months, but the increase was not significant.  Similarly, the ICRS Functional Knee Status was 
significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and even a bit higher at 24 months, but again, the 24 
month Functional Knee Status was not significantly different than the 12 month scores.

Knutsen et al. YEAR? described a randomized trial of 80 patients that compared ACI to microfracture.  
Both groups had significantly higher Lysholm scores and reduced pain at one and two year follow-up 
when compared to the baseline measurements, but there was no statistical difference between the 
groups.  The improvement in the Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36) score in the first two years was 
significantly higher for the microfracture group.  All other results from the two methods yielded similar 
clinical results. 
In a randomized trial comparing ACI to mosaicplasty, Bentley, et al. YEAR? found that the Cincinnati 
Rating Scores were better for ACI than mosaicplasty, but not statistically significant.  The study 
included an arthroscopic assessment at one year where ICRS repair scores were assigned.  Only 60 of 
the 100 patients (60%) returned for follow-up. There were 82% of the patients in the ACI group that had 
a repair score of good or excellent.  This is significantly higher than the 34% of the patients in the 
mosaicplasty group, with at least a good repair score.25  The study included an arthroscopic assessment at 
one year where ICRS repair scores were assigned.  Only 60 of the 100 patients (60%) returned for 
follow-up.  
In their 2017 meta-analysis, Schuette, et al. [21], guide their readers through a brief history of the 
evolution of ACI, a restorative approach to chondral defects.  They write: 
“ACI is a 2-step procedure in which chondrocytes are first arthroscopically harvested and cultured in 
vitro. The second procedure involves injecting the chondral defect with the cultured cells and then 
covering them with a periosteal patch (first-generation ACI) or collagen membrane (second-generation 
ACI). Issues negatively affecting clinical outcomes, such as periosteal patch hypertrophy associated with 
the first-generation ACI and extensive suturing and cell leakage associated with second generation ACI, 
have led to the development of third generation ACI, otherwise known as matrix-assisted autologous 
chondrocyte transplantation (MACT). In MACT, cultured chondrocytes are seeded into a matrix 
scaffold and then fixed to the chondral defect with fibrin glue. MACT was first introduced into clinical 
practice in Europe in 1998. Third-generation ACI was just recently approved by the Food and Drug 
Administration in the United States [MACI by Vericel, Inc., in December of 2016], with several 
additional clinical trials currently underway.” 
With both Carticel and MACI, the body of clinical evidence for autologous chondrocyte implantation 
was collected in larger defects of approximately 5 cm2, with concomitant procedures and previous 
microfacture failures, whereas current FDA guidance has required far stricter inclusion/exclusion 
criteria.  Upon approval of MACI by FDA, Vericel, Inc., chose to conclude the commercialization of 
Carticel in Summer of 2017, and the product is no longer sold to clinicians.  The underlying patient 
biopsies originally used for Carticel were transitioned to MACI upon commercialization in early 2017. 
7.3.2. 
MACI (Vericel, Inc.) 
In the MACI technique, in the initial arthroscopic procedure, chondrocytes are harvested from a 
non-weight-bearing articular surface and cultured ex vivo in a monolayer. These cultured chondrocytes 
are then seeded on one side of a membrane comprised of Type I and Type III porcine collagen.  During 
the second procedure, performed arthroscopically or via a mini-arthrotomy, the chondrocyte-seeded side 
of the membrane is placed against the subchondral bone surface and affixed using a fibrin glue [22]. 
As referenced earlier, MACI received FDA approval for US commercialization in December of 2016.  
Key clinical evidence for MACI came from the SUMMIT [Demonstrate the Superiority of MACI 
Implant to Microfracture Treatment] multi-center study, whose results were published by Saris, et al.

NeoCart (Histogenics, Inc.) 
Like MACI, the NeoCart product begins by harvesting healthy chondrocytes from a non-weight-bearing 
portion of the knee. Unlike MACI, however, these chondrocytes are cultured on a three-dimensional 
“honeycomb-like” bovine-derived Type I collagen scaffold within a low oxygen-tension custom 
bioreactor designed to mimic the intra-articular environment [22].  The goal is to create a 
neocartilaginous implant that possesses increased glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and type-II collagen 
production. Thus, instead of implanting cells with the potential to differentiate and form hyaline 
cartilage, NeoCart “is a matured tissue-like implant containing hyaline GAGs designed to provide a 
more rapid and potentially sustained therapeutic effect for articular cartilage repair” [24]. The NeoCart 
implant is secured to the subchondral bone using a proprietary resorbable tissue adhesive (CT3, 
Histogenics, Waltham, MA).

The role of Physical Therapy/Rehabilitiation 
All patients undergoing treatment for cartilage damage of the knee irrespective of treatment modality 
should undergo a monitored rehabilitation program to ensure optimum results. In the article, “Functional 
Outcomes after Surgical Management of Articular Cartilage Lesions in the Knee: A Systematic 
Literature Review to Guide Postoperative Rehabilitation,” Schmitt, et al. [16] conclude from their 
research, “Significant quadriceps femoris strength deficits, gait deviations, and functional deficits persist 
for 5 to 7 years following ACI and microfracture surgical procedures. Future research regarding 
rehabilitation interventions to help mitigate these deficits is warranted.” As detailed in articles by Wilk, 
et al. [17] and Mithoefer, et al. [18], optimal post-operative rehabilitation of the knee after articular 
cartilage repair should be individualized to the patient: tailored to the patient’s age and BMI, his/her 
defect size, depth, and location, the repair technique used, duration of symptoms prior to intervention, 
and evolving quality of the cartilage [18]. As both sets of researchers instruct, the phases of post-
operative physical therapy should mirror the biologic phase of wound repair: during Phase 1 
(proliferative phase) of cartilage repair, the initial healing benefits from a reduction in swelling and a 
gradual restoration of passive range of motion and weightbearing [17]. During Phase 2 (transition 
phase), a patient proceeds from gradual to full weightbearing with a focus on joint function restoration. 
During the final phase (remodeling/maturation), the goal is to have the patient return to full activity. 
Recognize the inherent variability associated with post-operative rehabilitation: failure to individualize 
treatment to the patient’s condition, and failure to match the strength and motion restoration to the 
evolving healing of the cartilage defect, can all lead to considerable variability in patient outcomes. 
Ebert, et al., [19] demonstrated that differences in rehabilitation regimens could alter the outcomes after 
chondral injury restoration using matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI, 
discussed below).above)  An accelerated weightbearing regimen (full weightbearing at 8 weeks 
post-procedure) was compared to a traditional regimen (full weightbearing at 11 weeks post-procedure) 
by measuring pain and various functional metrics at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-surgery.  Patients in 
the accelerated weightbearing regimen reported significantly lower pain and demonstrated improved 6-
minute walk distances compared to the those in the traditional rehabilitation regimen. While it is 
imperative to highlight that these patients received chondral restoration rather than microfracture – and 
recognizing that the needs of graft repair healing may be different –research by Ebert, et al., is meant to 
emphasize that differences in rehabilitation can affect surgical outcomes in treating chondral defects.   
That said, research by Marder et al. [20], suggested that the impact of rehabilitation on functional 
outcomes can be secondary to other, more significant factors. In their study, patients with focal full-
thickness chondral defects less than 2 cm2 treated with microfracture entered one of two rehabilation 
groups post-surgery: in one group, patients were treated with non-weight bearing and continuous passive 
motion (CPM) for six weeks, while in the second group, patients were allowed weight bearing as 
tolerated and did not use CPM. Outcomes were assessed using the Lysholm knee rating scale augmented 
by the Tegner method of activity evaluation. No significant difference was detected between the two 
groups when comparing the pre-operative and post-operative Lysholm scores. It is possible that the 
healing of small focal defects after microfracture is insensitive to differences in post-surgical 
rehabilitation.

was submitted to the IND under a Special Protocol Assessment request and was approved by FDA on 
March 10, 2009.The trial was required to be a prospective, multi-center randomized trial of superiority 
comparing the success of NeoCart to that of microfracture.  The primary endpoint was agreed upon to be 
one year with continuation through years 2 and 3. Although the trial was designed prior to the guidance 
document it complied with the requirement to demonstrate superiority and to have two different 
validated scores for pain and function endpoints to assess for meaningful improvement. The agreed upon 
endpoints were KOOS pain and IKDC subjective function scores which are very well accepted validated 
scoring systems for both pain and function of knee pathology. All KOOS and IKDC subscores were 
prospectively obtained at baseline and at all post-procedure visits 
The guidance document does not require that these two different tests be combined into a dual threshold 
primary responder analysis which was done in the NeoCart trial.  This addeds an additional hurdle as a 
patient was required to reach the success levels for both measures to be considered a positive responder. 
To meet the objectives the primary endpoint for the Phase III study was defined as a test of superiority 
(one-sided Pearson’s chi-square test, =0.025) vs microfracture, in terms of a composite clinical success 
(CCS) used in a dual threshold responder analysis for pain and function at 12-months post index 
surgery. A subject was considered a responder if they achieved both of the following outcomes: 
• An improvement of at least 12 points in outcome compared to baseline on the KOOS pain 
assessment test, and 
• An improvement of at least 20 points in outcome compared to baseline on the IKDC 
subjective test. 
These improvement thresholds were set based upon the available data at the time and above what are 
currently considered minimum clinically important differences (MCID) for improvements on pain and 
function as established in the literature. The MCID had not been well established at the time of the 
writing of the protocol and the thresholds were determined with considerable input from the 
performance in the Phase II study where microfracture performed poorly.  
The current standards for clinically meaningful IKDC scores start at a 6-point improvement as early as 6 
months and increase to 15 or 16 points at later timeframes.  For KOOS pain, the meaningful clinically 
important difference is seen in the 8 to 10-point range.  Both thresholds in the NeoCart trial (KOOS of 
12 points and IKDC of 20 points) were higher than what was and is now seen as a minimum clinically 
meaningful or important difference, or MCID (Collins, 2011). 
Microfracture was used as the concurrent control for the NeoCart Phase III study as it is the most 
common surgical treatment modality, and current standard of care both at the time of the study design 
and persistent today despite the limitations of the procedure as noted for both efficacy and durability. 
Microfracture continues to be used as both active and as an historical control in other ongoing studies 
for treatment of knee cartilage defects based upon FDA guidance. Despite extensive use of 
microfracture commercially over the last two decades in broad patient populations, a treatment effect in 
the population evaluated in this Phase III study is not well established due to a paucity of adequate and 
well-controlled studies that are designed in accordance to the now available FDA guidance. The sponsor 
established inclusion and exclusion criteria and a study population based on FDA and clinical expert 
feedback to provide the microfracture treatment the best possible chance to succeed and attempt to 
institute clinical equipoise for the study, as there are well-known limitations to this treatment. Key 
inclusion and exclusion criteria were lesions less than 6cm2, BMI less than 35, no concomitant knee 
surgical procedures, and no prior microfracture treatments allowed.

9.5.2. 
Arthroscopy Procedure 
The arthroscopy procedures were scheduled in order to allow ample time for lab processing, MRI image 
submission and core lab baseline letter return prior to the procedure. All required baseline results were 
available before the time of arthroscopy. Data was recorded during the procedure to document that the 
patient met the selection criteria. Data collection included assessments of all cartilage defects and status 
of all structures in the knee compartments. 
9.5.3. 
Biopsy Procedure 
The steps for the Biopsy Procedure were performed in accordance with the Instructions for Use (IFU), 
after patient randomization to the NeoCart cohort. 
9.5.4. 
Microfracture Procedure 
The following steps, described in more detail by Steadman, et al. [27], were performed after patient 
randomization to the microfracture cohort: 
a. Debride the lesion of all remaining unstable cartilage. All loose or marginally attached 
cartilage from the surrounding rim is to be debrided to form a stable, perpendicular edge of 
healthy, viable cartilage. 
b. A curette is used to carefully remove the calcified layer from the base of the lesion. The 
calcified cartilage comprises a layer between the deep zone of cartilage and the subchondral 
bone and this layer can increase in thickness with age. The calcified layer can be difficult to 
differentiate visually but can be distinguished more easily from the hard, underlying

Page 32 of 138 
 
CLINICAL STUDY REPORT 
subchondral bone plate by tactile feedback. The use of a curette provides better manual 
feedback than an arthroscopic shaver and reduces the risk of excessive debridement. 
c. Make multiple holes in the exposed subchondral bone plate using an arthroscopic awl. A 
Linvatec Corp. awl is recommended. The holes should be made perpendicular to the surface. 
d. Microfracture holes should initially be made around the periphery immediately adjacent to 
the healthy stable cartilage, and then progressing toward the center of the lesion. The holes 
should be made 3-4 mm apart and should be to a depth of 2 to 4 mm. A minimum spacing 
should be maintained so that one hole does not break into another and damage the 
subchondral plate between holes. There should be visible marrow fat droplets and blood 
released from the microfracture holes. 
e. Evacuate all fluid and close the access sites without placement of intra-articular drains and 
dress the incision following standard hospital procedures. 
f. Post-surgical recovery care was conducted in accordance with standard hospital procedures 
and the patient is to be discharged at the discretion of the investigator. 
9.5.5. 
NeoCart Implant Procedure 
The NeoCart derived from the biopsy sample was intended to be implanted into the same patient. 
Therefore, utmost care was taken to match the identity of the patient to the patient indicated on the 
NeoCart label. An arthrotomy procedure was required for NeoCart implantation into the defect bed. The 
following steps were followed during the implant procedure: 
1. The patient was prepared for arthrotomy using conventional preparation. Standard 
hospital procedures were followed to gain access to the defect. 
2. Any fragments and debris from the defect were removed and the defect bed was 
smoothed. The zone of calcified cartilage was carefully scraped away taking care not to penetrate the 
subchondral bone. A tourniquet was not used during the procedure so that inadvertent bleeding from the 
subchondral bone could be ascertained and stopped prior to the implantation of the NeoCart. 
3. The NeoCart was removed from the shipping container. The size and shape of the defect to be treated 
were determined and the NeoCart was trimmed to provide an implant piece that fit the defect 
dimensions. The trimmed NeoCart was then positioned into the defect to confirm the NeoCart fit. 
4. A CT3 resorbable tissue adhesive kit was then opened and prepared. The CT3 was used within 20 
minutes, or the material was discarded and new CT3 mixed. 
5. A small amount of CT3 was evenly spread into the defect bed, and then the trimmed NeoCart implant 
was placed. 
6. After NeoCart placement, moderate pressure was briefly applied to the implant to allow the CT3 to 
set. The NeoCart implant was then affixed to the defect. (The NeoCart implant was not to be 
repositioned after initial placement.) 
7. A thin layer of CT3 was spread over the NeoCart and also extended the CT3 layer onto the native 
articular cartilage surface. The CT3 was to extend at least 2 mm past the NeoCart around the periphery 
of the defect. The surface of the CT3 was also to be as smooth as possible, without being proud in 
relation to the surrounding articular cartilage. 
8. The Curing Component buffer was applied to the CT3 and the CT3 was allowed time to set. The 
setting time was accelerated by the use of the buffer. Any excess CT3 was trimmed to create a smooth 
surface. 
9. Following the surface application of CT3, the leg was carefully extended to avoid 
excessive shear stresses on the NeoCart. No range of motion evaluations were performed, and additional 
flexing of the knee was to be avoided.

procedures. A brace was applied to immobilize the knee and locked at an angle

location. The patient was then fitted with anti-embolism stockings to minimize the risk of embolism.

Rehabilitation 
Rehabilitation was guided by the investigator in general phases described below and advanced according 
to each patient’s specific issues (healing and function). The primary driver of the very proscriptive 
rehabilitation protocol was the microfracture procedure and the seminal work by Dr. Steadman 
regarding how to optimize success of microfracture. This rehabilitation plan was individualized, phased 
and included a detailed description of activities and limitations.  It that incorporated specific 
strengthening and conditioning goals to be attained prior to advancing to the next phase of rehabilitation 
and to facilitate successful recovery from surgery, keeping in mind the patient’s goals and previous 
activity level. Exercises were specified, and patients trained to complete the exercises, but the specific 
exercises and training on how to perform the exercises was done at the discretion of the investigator. 
Patients were contacted periodically for reinforcement and support in the performance of the exercises. 
Use of Knee Brace: 
Patients with condylar lesions in either study arm were not required to wear a knee brace but may have 
been prescribed a brace at the investigator’s discretion. Patients with trochlear lesions should have been 
placed in a locking brace immediately and for at least 6 weeks post-operatively, with the unlocking 
schedule determined by the investigator. If the investigator prescribed a knee brace for patients, this was 
documented in the patient’s file. 
Prophylaxis for Thromboembolic Disease (TED): 
For any patient placed into a knee immobilizer or partially- or fully-locked knee brace following any 
study procedure, two methods of thromboembolic disease (TED) prophylaxis, aspirin and a thigh-high 
or knee-high compression stocking for the operative extremity, was ordered for the duration of 
immobilization/bracing. The dosage of aspirin and the period of daily use of compression stockings was 
determined by the investigator. 
Continuous passive motion therapy (CPM): 
Continuous passive motion therapy (CPM) began on the day of the procedure for all patients not placed 
into a knee immobilizer or hinged knee brace with restricted motion. For patients placed into a knee 
brace or immobilizer, and at the discretion of the investigator, CPM began as early as the day of the 
procedure but, in any case, no later than the first post-operative visit. CPM continued for a minimum of 
6 weeks and a maximum of 8 weeks. All patients were recommended to perform CPM for 6-10 hours 
per day, but investigators could alter the daily amount based on each patient’s needs. 
Weightbearing Status: 
NeoCart patients with small condylar lesions that were less than 2cm2 with a circumferentially stable 
margin of intact cartilage were limited to toe touch weightbearing until the first post-operative visit (10 
days) and increased weightbearing as tolerated after that visit.

NeoCart patients with condylar lesions that were greater than or equal to 2 cm2 or with lesions that do 
not have a circumferentially stable margin of intact cartilage were limited to toe-touch weightbearing for 
4-6 weeks after implant and then increased weightbearing as tolerated. 
Microfracture patients with condylar lesions were limited to toe-touch weightbearing for a minimum of 
6-8 weeks. 
Both NeoCart and microfracture patients with trochlear lesions were allowed weightbearing as tolerated 
with a brace. If a patient had lesions treated on both the trochlea and condyle, the early weightbearing 
status defaulted to the most conservative, i.e., toe touch weightbearing for 6 weeks, while range of 
motion rehabilitation mirrored that typically prescribed for trochlear lesions. 
Rehabilitation StagesPhases: 
Phase 1 – Protection, Edema Management, Range of Motion (RoM), Muscle Activation (initiated 
after the first post-operative visit through 6-8 weeks post-operatively) 
Rehabilitation in this phase focused on gentle restoration of knee motion without the use of resistance 
(e.g., stationary bike with no load). For patients who begin weightbearing as tolerated in this phase 
(NeoCart patients with small condylar lesions and all patients with trochlear lesions), the investigator 
considered judicious and limited advancement of rehabilitation to assist with restoration of normal gait, 
avoiding strenuous motion and strengthening exercises aimed at preparation for functional activities. 
Phase 2 - RoM, Gait training, Knee Control (initiated 6-8 weeks post-operatively dependent upon 
progress at 6 week follow-up visit and advancement over 6-8 weeks) 
Rehabilitation in this phase focused on more advanced range of motion exercises and closed chain 
exercises to assist with resumption of normal gait and to prepare for functional activities (e.g., stationary 
biking with progressive resistance, water program, resistance tubing exercises). 
Phase 3 - Strength and Balance (initiated 12-16 weeks post-operatively dependent upon progress 
at 3 month follow-up visit and continued with advancement to at least 6 months post-operatively) 
Rehabilitation in this phase focused on improving strength, endurance and proprioception (e.g., free 
weights, machine weights). 
Phase 4 - Sport Specific Training and Participation (initiated no earlier than 6 months post-
operatively and dependent upon progress at 6 month follow-up visit) 
Rehabilitation in this phase focused on more advanced strengthening, endurance and proprioceptive 
exercises and on return to patient-specific sporting activities (e.g., pivoting, cutting, jumping).

9.5.7. 
Efficacy Parameters 
The primary efficacy study endpoint was defined as a test of superiority (one-sided Pearson’s Chi-
squareT test, =0.025) vs microfracture, in terms of a composite clinical success (CCS) used in a dual-
threshold responder analysis based on improvement in knee-specific pain and function at 1 year using 
the IKDC Subjective knee exam and the Pain domain score from the KOOS Knee Injury and 
Osteoarthritis Outcome Score. 
Patients were required to demonstrate both an improvement in KOOS pain of ≥ 12 points and IKDC 
subjective score of ≥ 20 points to be a positive responder. 
The IKDC instrument is a validated region-specific patient-oriented outcome measure of symptoms, 
function, and sports activity.  A score of 100 represents no limitation with activities of daily living or 
sports activities and absence of symptoms.  The normative score for this age group is about 90. 
The KOOS has five separate scores: Pain, Symptoms, Activities of Daily Living (ADL), 
Sport/Recreation, and Quality of Life (QoL).  Similar to IKDC, a KOOS Pain score of 100 represents no 
pain.  The KOOS Pain assessment is preferred over a VAS Pain scale (to be evaluated in supporting 
analyses) because it evaluates pain levels using a pain frequency scale (never, rarely, sometimes, often, 
always) in relation to specific knee activities of daily living (e.g. walking, climbing, sitting, pivoting, 
etc.). 
The dual threshold is a composite score inclusive of the IKDC subjective and KOOS pain values.  By 
The two sub-scores were used as the primary endpoint whiledefinition this means that all individual 
IKDC and KOOS endpoints were prospectively collected both as exploratory analyses and for purposes 
of conducting the dual-threshold responder analysis. 
The secondary efficacy endpoints included time to full weight-bearing, ‘Treatment failure’ (defined as 
>8-point deterioration in KOOS Pain score at 1 year compared to baseline) and the presence of mature 
collagen layering as assessed by MRI T2 mapping at 1 year.

Determination of Sample Size 
The initial sample size was selected to be 245 subjects (approximately 163 NeoCart subjects and 82 Mfx 
subjects). With a sample size of 163 NeoCart subjects and 82 Mfx subjects, the power is 86%, assuming 
a one-sided test for superiority based on the chi-square test, a one-sided alpha level of 0.025, and true 
responder rates of 0.70 and 0.50 for the NeoCart and Mfx treatments, respectively.  
Specifically, a two group 2 test with a 0.025 one-sided significance level had 86% power to detect the 
difference between an Mfx responder rate of Mfx  = 0.50 and a NeoCart responder rate of NeoCart = 0.70 
(odds ratio of 2.33) when the sample sizes are 163 and 82, respectively (a total sample size of 245) 
[Elashoff, 2007i].  With an assumed 7% lost to follow-up rate by 1 year, the expected number of 
subjects was 228 (152 NeoCart subjects and 76 Mfx subjects), and the power of the test for superiority 
was 83%.

9.7.5.6. 
Analysis of MRI Data 
All MRI images collected under this protocol were submitted to the MRI Core Lab. The MRI Core Lab 
was blinded to the randomization arm. Analysis included standard MRI review to assess the quantity of 
the defect repair during the course of the trial. These MRI findings are divided into anatomic 
assessments that were made using generally accepted, well-established MRI sequences, and more 
advanced sequences that allow for the direct, qualitative assessment of the area of defect repair. 
Standard MRI sequences provide high contrast between fat suppressed bone and cartilage; however, 
they are not fluid sensitive and are degraded in the postoperative setting due to susceptibility artifact. 
Fast spin echo sequences with high in-plane resolution provide good cartilage to fluid contrast, making 
them more sensitive to partial thickness lesions. 
In addition to standard MRI review, an advanced T2 MRI image acquisition sequence was used at 
qualified MRI centers. T2 mapping permits direct, qualitative and quantitative assessment of the 
collagen component of the extracellular matrix of the NeoCart implant and adjacent articular cartilage. 
T2 relaxation time is a reproducible MRI parameter that reflects the internuclear reaction, or dephasing, 
that occurs as a result of transverse relaxation of the excited hydrogen dipoles. The stratification of the 
T2 signal is indicative of a normal arrangement of the type II collagen fibers within the cartilage repair.

9.7.6. 
Handling of Dropouts or Missing Data 
Multiple imputation was specified to be used in sensitivity analyses to determine Month 12 responder 
status when Month 12 CCS was missing. In this approach, “Prediction is based on the patient level of 
success and failure—not on the two components of success separately.” 
However, statistical efficiencies can be obtained by using linear regression based multiple imputation 
[29-32] on the underlying continuous variables of change in KOOS and change IKDC subjective scores 
separately, rather than on an endpoint defined by collapsing multiple underlying continuous variables. 
Therefore, missing Month 12 KOOS and IKDC were individually imputed as continuous variables in 
parallel imputations and then combined to form the CCS. This approach takes advantage of potentially 
stronger associations among continuous variables. Also, multiple imputation of the individual scores is 
closer to the LOCF approach specified for the primary analysis. In the primary analysis, LOCF was 
applied to KOOS pain and IKDC subjective score individually, and then each score is to be 
dichotomized in order to form the composite clinical endpoint. 
The original plan included varying certain model parameters to reflect extremes concerning the impact 
of missing values on group differences. This type of analysis was retained but was accomplished using 
conventional tipping point analyses. 
9.7.6.1. 
Responder analysis 
When computing responder status in primary analyses, e.g., 1-year composite clinical success in the 
intent-to-treat (ITT) (as well as in the As-Treated (AT) analyses), the last-observation carried-forward 
(LOCF) method were used to impute the components of missing KOOS and IKDC. That is, subjects 
missing 1-year values had their 1 year values replaced by their Month 6 values, if Month 6 was 
available. If Month 6 is not available, then the Month 3 values were used. If there are no values past 
baseline, the subject was considered a Month 12 nonresponder in primary efficacy analyses in the ITT 
analysis set. 
Sensitivity analyses based on multiple imputation and on ‘tipping point’ analyses will also be 
performed. 
9.7.6.2. 
Analysis of mean changes 
Supporting analyses involving group comparisons in mean changes will involve the use of mixed model 
repeated measures (MMRM) which allows inclusion of all available data including intermediate values 
of KOOS Pain and IKDC Subjective score changes as well as relevant baseline covariates to inform the 
contrast of interest.  
Covariates will include age, gender, total lesion size at arthroscopy, total lesion size at treatment, BMI, 
number of study lesions, injury type, most severe lesion ICRS grade, and smoking status. Last-
observation-carried-forward imputation will also be conducted for the specified secondary efficacy 
endpoints. If a patient has no results post-baseline for T2 mapping, they were excluded from analysis. 
For all other endpoints and outcomes, there was no imputation of missing data with the exception of 
analysis done on the questionnaires added in version 7 of the protocol and the new exploratory analyses

9.7.6.3. 
Multiple imputation 
Multiple imputation was used as an alternative to LOCF for imputing missing 1-year responder status in 
sensitivity analyses for the primary efficacy endpoint. Section 8 provides details concerning the methods 
to be used. Three questionnaires were added to the study with the approval of version 7 of the protocol 
(December 12, 2014). Due to the timing of the addition of these questionnaires, patients enrolled under 
earlier versions of the protocol are missing these questionnaires at baseline and any other visits attended 
prior to version 7. For this questionnaire data, missing values were imputed up to 1-year using 
regression based on available timepoints through PROC MI. Multiply imputed inferences from the 
unadjusted mean differences and the MMRM mean differences were pooled together using PROC 
MIANALYZE in order to create combined results for each. As more patients were enrolled under 
versions 7 and 8 of the protocol and fewer patients enrolled under those versions have reached 2-3-year 
visit windows at the time of submission, extended follow-up visit responses will not be analyzed for 
Marx activity rating, EQ-5D-5L, or WPAI. 
9.7.7. 
Interim Analyses 
The original study design included a formal interim analysis to be conducted based on 80-90% of the 
originally planned sample for the purpose of sample size re-estimation. There was no provision for early 
stopping for superiority.  The interim analysis for sample size re-estimation was not performed as the 
rate of lost to follow-up (the only nuisance parameter) was lower than anticipated (2.4% by Jan 2017 
rather than 7%), and the sponsor decided not to conduct the interim analysis for sample size re-
estimation. 
Additionally, the original study design included a pre-planned administrative analysis to be conducted 
“for the sponsor's financial planning purposes with results potentially provided to a small number of 
individuals responsible for company financing”. This was specified to occur when “~75% of patients 
have been enrolled”. No specific statistical analysis was specified for this ‘administrative analysis’. 
The rigor of this planned “administrative analysis” had been enhanced by pre-planning of a futility 
analysis based on the determination of conditional power. To this end, a futility analysis was planned 
take place after 50% of the initially planned sample size (i.e., 123 patients) was due for their month 12 
follow-up visit.  
However, the iSAP stipulated that the futility analysis “may not be conducted if enrollment is completed 
or nearly completed by the time that 50% of patients are evaluable for the Month 12 study success 
criterion,” At the time that approximately 50% of the patients were evaluable for the success criterion, 
the study enrollment was almost completd, and the sponsor decided not to conduct the administratieve 
futility analysis.

Safety Analysis 
9.7.10.1. Extent of Exposure 
The Safety Population includes all patients who were consented, enrolled and randomized into the 
clinical study.  Patients who were randomized into the NeoCart arm but not implanted with the NeoCart 
construct were followed for safety events through standard post-operative follow-up for arthroscopy. 
Safety events were classified by the AT population to ensure that the one patient who was randomized to 
the NeoCart arm but declined a repeat biopsy and underwent microfracture would have potential events 
captured under the correct treatment. 
9.7.10.2. Adverse Events 
For each safety analysis in which the outcome is an event (possibly composite), treatment groups were 
compared using counts and percentages. 
Only treatment-emergent AEs were analyzed. AEs were coded using the Medical Dictionary for 
Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 17. The number and percentage of patients with at least one 
adverse event, at least one serious adverse event (SAE), and at least one procedure related adverse event 
were presented by treatment group. The number and percentage of patients with at least one NeoCart 
related adverse event were presented for the NeoCart treatment group. AEs that are definitely, probably, 
or possibly related to the procedure, or for which the relationship to the procedure is missing, were 
considered procedure related, and AEs that are definitely, probably, or possibly related to NeoCart, or 
for which the relationship to NeoCart is missing, were considered NeoCart related. AEs and SAEs are 
summarized at the patient level by MedDRA system organ class (SOC) and preferred term using 
frequencies and percentages. AEs will also be tabulated at the event level by severity and by relationship 
to the procedure for each treatment group, and by relationship to NeoCart for the NeoCart treatment 
group.  
All Adverse Events were captured during the study independent of relatedness to the treatment arm or 
procedure.  Events were assessed by the principal investigator for causality and relatedness to either the 
procedure or the implant or both. Summaries were restricted to Treatment Emergent Adverse Events 
(TEAEs), which were defined as those AEs that occurred after the start of the arthroscopic procedure or 
worsened during the study. Verbatim terms were mapped to preferred terms and System Organ Classes 
using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) dictionary (version 17.

population are presented in Table 17.  
The majority of patients had a single study lesion in the index knee (NeoCart 84.1%, 
microfracture 91.1%).  The most common additional procedure performed was partial 
meniscectomy (24.7% NeoCart and 26.6% microfracture).  The median % of meniscus 
remaining in both arms was 90%. The arthroscopic evaluation results for the mITT, AT, and PP 
populations are located in Appendix.

Primary Endpoint

• An improvement of at least 12 points in outcome compared to baseline on the KOOS 
pain assessment test, and  
• An improvement of at least 20 points in outcome compared to baseline on the IKDC 
subjective test.

11.1.2.1. Lesion size 
With regard to lesion size, the NeoCart arm performed similarly across the entire study 
population (Table 26).  However, there was a clear differentiation of microfracture in smaller 
lesion sizes only, with NeoCart showing statisticially significant superiority in lesions greater 
than 2.2 cm2 for the ITT population and greater than 1.6 cm2 for the mITT population. The 
mean lesion size for the study was 2.2 cm2, and for all lesions greater than that, NeoCart patients 
had a composite success rate of 71.7.% while the microfracture success rate was only 51.5% 
(p=0.0050) at 1 year for the ITT population.  Evaluation of the earlier timepoint of 6 months 
demonstrated potential earlier pain relief and functional improvements, for lesions greater than 
1.8 cm2 in the NeoCart arm. , At 6 months,NeoCart patients had a composite success rate of 
59.5% while the microfracture success rate was only 40.5% (p=0.0177) at 1 year for the ITT 
population. 
Similar to the relative performance in lesion sizes between NeoCart and microfracture, literature 
suggests that patient who have increased BMI demonstrate worse results with microfracture.  
Tables X & Y illustrate the impact of weight (BMI) on the 1-year primary efficacy endpoint with 
NeoCart performing equally across the different weight categories with a highly statistically 
significant improvement when compared to microfracture for those patients with a BMI of 28 or 
more.  As noted above, microfracture is known to perform better in lower weight and younger 
patients.  This has relevance in the United States as a BMI of greater than 24.9 is considered 
obese.  Clinicians must take into account the limitations of a treatment that is impacted by weight 
in such a negative fashion, and regularly exclude such patients from receiving microfracture in 
their clinical practice. 
In an effort to better understand if there was a specific lesion size cut-off where NeoCart and MF 
performed equally well below the mean lesion size of 2.2cm2 the data was analyzed in 0.2cm2 
increments and is presented in Table 26.  For the ITT population statistical significance of 
superiority of the NeoCart arm is reached at the 2.2cm lesion size.  In the mITT population 
which represents those patients who actually received the NeoCart treatment there is a high 
degree of statistical superiority across all lesion sizes.

Time to full weight-bearing 
The time to full weight bearing (median days) at 1 year was 51 for NeoCart and 51 for 
Microfracture(p<0.6833). While the Kaplan-Meier curve demonstrated that more patients were 
able to full weight bear earlier with NeoCart there was no statistically significant difference 
between the groups. These values may not represent a true picture of time to weight bearing for 
several reasons, first the protocol required a very proscriptive rehabilitation plan to limit patients 
from being full weight bearing early as this variable has been shown to be associated with worse 
outcomes in the microfracture group.  This is an absolute necessity for the microfracture arm 
success to prevent dislodgement of the mesenchymal stem cell rich clot.  For the NeoCart arm 
the articular cartilage graft is secure in the defect with the adhesive preventing dislodgement,

11.2.3. 
MRI Data 
MRIs were obtained at the timepoints noted in Table 4 (Baseline, 6months, 1 year and then 
annually. The baseline MRI included the following views: Both legs, standing, full extension 
from femoral head to tibial malleolus, anterio-posterior, 450 flexion, weight bearing, postero-
anterior and merchant view-300 flexion. The post procedure exam was a standard MRI and time 
for 63% of transverse relaxation read (T2) image acquisition to be performed at sites where T2 
software was available. 
All MRI images were submitted to the MRI Core Laboratory. Analysis included standard MRI 
review to assess the quality of the NeoCart implant and microfracture during the course of the

trial. These MRI findings were divided into anatomic assessments that were made using 
generally accepted, well-established MRI sequences and more advanced sequences that allowed 
for the direct, qualitative assessment of both the area of NeoCart implant or microfracture. 
In addition to standard MRI review, an advanced T2 mapping MRI sequence was obtained to 
evaluate for qualitative and quantitative assessment of the collagen component of the 
extracellular matrix of the NeoCart implant and adjacent articular cartilage. Standard MRI 
sequences provided high contrast between fat suppressed bone and cartilage; however, they are 
generally not fluid sensitive and are degraded in the postoperative setting due to susceptibility 
artifact. Fast spin echo sequences with high in-plane resolution provide good cartilage to fluid 
contrast, making them more sensitive to partial thickness lesions. 
T2 relaxation time is a reproducible MRI parameter that reflects the internuclear reaction, or 
dephasing, that occurs as a result of transverse relaxation of the excited hydrogen dipoles. The 
stratification of T2 reflects the arrangement of the type II collagen fibers within the matrix. T2 
mapping of articular cartilage at clinical field strengths reflects collagen fiber. Standardized 
regions of interest T2 mapping analysis was performed in the basilar and superficial halves of the 
area of NeoCart implant or microfracture, comparing this to T2 values in the adjacent cartilage 
that appears normal on standardized fast spin echo techniques. Particular attention was paid to 
the presence or absence of the zonal stratification of T2 of the area of the NeoCart implant or 
microfracture compared to the patient’s native hyaline cartilage. This allowed the Core Lab to 
possibly determine whether the NeoCart implant formed repair cartilage with collagen 
orientation and T2 values similar to hyaline cartilage and the nature of the cartilage that formed 
as the result of the microfracture procedure. 
At one year the MRI imaging results were similar between the two treatment arms with slightly 
more lesions being graded isointense in the NeoCart arm than the microfracture arm (37.5% vs 
24.7%) and slightly more lesions being graded hypointense in the microfracture arm 27.2% vs 
15.8%). Integration of the defect area was similar as well as the percentage with 67-100% fill 
(58.7 % NeoCart and 54.3% microfracture). Both groups had minimal hypertrophy, 
displacement, subchondral edema and similar scoring of bony overgrowth. 
While T2 mapping has been thought to help determine the progression to mature hyaline 
cartilage there were no statistically significant differences in the relaxation time means for the 
superficial or deep layers or their standard deviations. The relaxation times at 6 months for the 
superficial cartilage was similar between treatment arms (62.5077msec NeoCart, 62.9531msec 
microfracture p=0.8191) The deep layer showed longer times for NeoCart while not statistically 
significant (57.4107 NeoCart vs 54.9544 msec microfracture p=0.2212).  The one-year data 
showed a slight decrease in the relaxation times as would be expected for organizing tissue but 
there was no difference between the groups, and both were about 10msec longer than the normal 
tissue.  Similar results were seen in the smaller Phase II study. Thus, for the NeoCart phase III 
clinical study MRI including T2 mapping provided minimal additional insigh into the healing 
process.

11.4. 
Efficacy Conclusions 
NeoCart did not demonstrate statistically superior performance with the dual threshold responder 
analysis missing by approximately 2 patients. However, when the data is reviewed a number of 
very important conclusions can be drawn. First that for the independent scores of KOOS pain 
and IKDC NeoCart does demonstrate a clinically and statistically significance at both the 6m and 
1 year time points. In addition, when the data is stratified by lesion size the performance 
separation is apparent at low lesion sizes and continues as lesion sizes increase.The primary 
endpoint for the Phase 3 clinical trial was a dual-threshold responder analysis measuring the 
improvement in KOOS pain and IKDC function scores for each patient treated with NeoCart 
compared to those treated with microfracture one year after the time of treatment. In clinical 
trials a threshold response is a way to take a continuous primary efficacy measure and 
dichotomize it into responders and non-responders.  The threshold is set based upon expectations 
for what a clinically meaningful result would be. In a dual threshold endpoint, the subjects must 
meet the value set as a responder both of two different measurements to be considered a 
responder (often termed a super superiority trial). At the time of the NeoCart phase 3 clinical 
trial design and discussion with the agency for the special protocol assessment (SPA) there was 
limited data available regarding what was a clinically meaningful change from baseline for either 
KOOS or IKDC and there had not been any completed prospective randomized trials.  As the 
field has evolved, clinicians have worked hard to identify the scores at which meaningful benefit

The NeoCart efficacy results from the pivotal study are clinically meaningful and relevant and

12. 
SAFETY EVALUATION 
12.1. 
Extent of exposure 
The NeoCart implant is (Cultured Autologous Neo-Cartilage) tissue implant is a 3-dimensional, 
white, opalescent disc (6cm2 area, 1.5to 2.0mm thick) designed to treat symptomatic defects of 
the articular cartilage of the knee.  Patients in the clinical trial undergo standard arthroscopy and 
if randomized to the NeoCart arm a biopsy of normal cartilage is obtained. This biopsy is then 
used to create the autologous cartilage graft that is placed into the defect at a second procedure 
approximately 8 weeks after the biopsy.  Patients randomized to the control arm have the 
microfracture procedure performed at the time of arthroscopy and are exposed to a single 
operative procedure. NeoCart patients are required to undergo a mini-arthrotomy second 
procedure for preparation and placement of the graft into the defect.  Patients in the NeoCart arm 
are exposed to the implant and an adhesive used to affix the implant.  Safety data is collected for 
all patients in both arms of the study for the duration of three years post baseline entry into the 
study with the follow-up for patients in the NeoCart arm continued through three years post 
implantation. 
12.2. 
Adverse events 
12.2.1. 
Brief summary of adverse events 
There were no unexpected safety events reported in either arm of the study. NeoCart and 
microfracture procedures were tolerated equally well with a low number of adverse events 
related to the study procedure (Table of TAES-15 in BB). Treatment emergent adverse events 
(TEAEs) are all adverse events that occur during the study period independent of relatedness to 
procedure or treatment. There were 12 serious TEAEs in the NeoCart arm (6.8%) and 6 in the 
microfracture group (7.5%; Table 27). TEAEs were similarly equal in both arms and observed in 
151 patients (445 events), (622% of the NeoCart population and 58.8% of the microfracture 
p=0.4808. 
The two most common adverse events were arthralgia (NeoCart 24.5% and microfracture 
(23.8%) and joint swelling (NeoCart 13.6%, microfracture 7.5%). The only other adverse event 
that occurred above a 5% rate was headache (NeoCart 11.1% and microfracture (12.5%). The 
vast majority of adverse events were of short duration and self limited. There were 4 deep vein 
thromboses in the NeoCart group and none in the microfracture arm (p=0.3052) and one 
pulmonary embolism in a patient randomized to the NeoCart arm.

13. 
DISCUSSION AND OVERALL CONCLUSIONS 
13.1. 
Discussion 
NeoCart’s clinical effectiveness was demonstrated through clinically meaningful and statistically 
significant treatment related improvements in pain and function at the 1-year timepoint versus 
the microfracture control arm. 
These data were generated from the largest adequate and well-controlled Phase III clinical study 
to date in a U.S representative patient population with stringent inclusion/exclusion standards 
based on FDA’s input. The efficacy of NeoCart was measured using validated and FDAaccepted 
instruments such as KOOS pain and IKDC function that that can be directly correlated to 
clinically relevant benefits for patients. 
NeoCart’s safety was also established, with TEAEs and TESAEs occurring in comparable rates 
in both arms of the study with no unexpected TEAEs or TESAEs. NeoCart has a positive 
benefit/risk profile in the knee cartilage defect space, where treatment options are limited to treat 
pain and loss of function  
The Phase 3 Clinical Trial of NeoCart did not meet the primary endpoint of a statistically 
significant superiority in pain and function in a dual threshold responder analysis 1 year after 
treatment as compared to microfracture. (Show table 14.2.11 Primary efficacy endpoint ITT 
population). However this failure to reach statistical significance in no way diminishes the facts 
that NeoCart provides a better alternative for the treatment of focal cartilage defects in the knee 
than current standard procedures.  In the Phase III clinical trial the NeoCart treatment arm 
performed better than anticipated based upon what was predicted from the results of the Phase II 
clinical trial and in the statistical plan (74% success compared to 70% anticipated). Microfracture 
performed worse than NeoCart but better than was anticipated based upon the Phase II clinical 
results, what has been observed in clinical practice and what was in the statistical plan (62% vs 
the expected 50%). Thus, the pre-specified difference of approximately 15-20% was not attained 
and a statistically significant result for the total population was just missed (p=0.074 Pearson’s 
chi-square for the ITT population and p=0.0257 for the mITT population). 
The early benefit of the NeoCart arm is across all treatment groups and is sustained through the 
1-year primary endpoint further reinforcing the durability of replacing a cartilage defect with a 
predictable cartilage tissue construct as opposed to chondrocytes. The results with respect to the 
primary endpoint (dual-threshold responder analysis 1 year after treatment) are provided for the 
ITT population, mITT population, and the PP population in Table 24, Table 25, and Error! 
Reference source not found., respectively. 
The NeoCart efficacy results from the pivotal study are clinically meaningful and relevant and 
should be put into the context of how the field of treatment for knee cartilage defects has evolved 
over the past 10 years since the NeoCart trial was designed. The NeoCart treatment group 
demonstrates a statistically significant improvement using the dual-threshold responder criteria at 
6 months and continues to improve numerically to the one-year primary endpoint mark (Table 
4), although not meeting the prespecified statistical superiority p-value. NeoCart treatment also 
demonstrated improvement with statistically significance over the microfracture group for the 
majority of both the KOOS and IKDC subgroup analyses when measured independently as 
reflected in current FDA Guidance. The early benefit of the NeoCart arm is across all treatment

groups and is sustained through the 1-year primary endpoint further reinforcing the durability of 
replacing a cartilage defect with a predictable cartilage tissue construct as opposed to 
chondrocytes. In addition, from a “do no harm” perspective it is important to evaluate the safety 
performance of those patients who not only had positive results even if they did not meet the 
dual threshold responder criteria but those who appeared to respond poorly after treatment.   
There are two previously FDA cleared or approved products for knee cartilage injuries (Carticel 
and MACI). Both products harvest healthy cartilage and then amplify the cells and return them to 
the area of the cartilage defect, Carticel as a cell suspension and MACI as a cell suspension 
seeded on a porcine collagen membrane. Carticel is no longer on the US market. There are 
fundamental differences between NeoCart and MACI product characteristics that may show 
distinct clinical advantages over time. NeoCart is a more mature cartilage tissue graft when it is 
implanted into the patient, rather than cells laid upon a collagen membrane. This is thought to 
account for the faster and potentially greater durability in result for patients. The demographics 
of the NeoCart phase III clinical study were different from those studied in the MACI Phase III 
SUMMIT clinical study that limit the ability for a direct comparison between these products. The 
lower limit of lesion sizes for inclusion in the Summit trial was 3.0cm2 and the mean lesion size 
was 4.8cm2 whereas in the NeoCart study the mean lesion size was 2.2cm2 with lesions treated 
from 0.5cm2 to 6cm2. This is important as microfracture treatment effect is known to perform 
better in smaller lesion sizes. 
The SUMMIT trial also reported on the KOOS subscales with the co-primary using the pain and 
function (sports and recreation subscale) at the two-year timepoint, versus the 1-year timepoint 
for NeoCart. Finally, the trial also allowed concomitant procedures (>30%) making it difficult to 
assign benefit to the primary cartilage defect repair in those patients and included previous 
microfracture treatments (>30%), which is known to result in poor subsequent outcomes and 
durability. The SUMMIT trial was conducted entirely in Europe with a 100% Caucasian 
demographic. The NeoCart Phase III study was conducted in the United States and Canada with 
almost 9% African American and almost 9% Hispanic patients which is more reflective of the 
U.S. population.  
Since 2014, at least four Phase III or Pivotal clinical trials for knee cartilage have been initiated 
by other third parties to our knowledge based on publicly available information. One trial 
(NOVOCART) is being conducted under an IND as a biologic or combination product, and the 
other three products (Hyalofast, GelrinC, Agili-C) are medical devices in clinical studies being 
performed under IDEs. All of these trials appear to have similar pain and function primary 
endpoints using measures of KOOS and/or IKDC either individually or as co-primary endpoints, 
designed as superiority trials with microfacture as the active control, or more recently a historical 
control arm, with 2-year endpoints, and a three year follow up period.  
Unlike the MACI trial, these trials also suggest that previous microfracture or other invasive 
surgeries should be excluded along with concomitant procedures and be limited to smaller 
lesions such as in the NeoCart trials. We also understand from publicly available information 
that each of these trials have had substantial difficulty in enrolling patients, similar to the 
sponsor’s lengthy experience. The narrow inclusion/exclusion criteria as seen in the NeoCart 
study, as well as public perceptions regarding the utility and efficacy of microfracture, have 
continued to make these trials both financially and logistically challenging.

There were a few patients that did not respond favorably in both treatment arms. From a “do no 
harm” perspective it is important to evaluate the safety performance of those patients who not 
only had positive results even if they did not meet the dual threshold responder criteria but those 
who appeared to respond poorly after treatment. There was a very large difference between the 
treatment arms who reported worse outcomes after the procedure with 12.7% of microfracture 
compared to 2.5% in the NeoCart arm on the IKDC function scales. Getting patients back to 
good functional performance is key both from a quality of life point of view and an ability to 
perform daily activities including driving a car, climbing stairs and being able to work. When 
evaluating the risk/benefit of the procedures there are several elements that demonstrate that the 
NeoCart procedure is unique to other knee cartilage repair options and are supported by the data. 
These are elective procedures with the overall goal of decreasing pain and improving the 
functional status of patients. The potential to impact long term function and decrease the 
progression to osteoarthritis and reduce the need for joint replacement surgery remains to be seen 
but has never been demonstrated with the alternative therapy of microfracture due to the eventual 
failure rate over time (Solheim, 2018). The process of taking a patient’s own cartilage and 
amplifying it within a scaffold under the conditions present in the knee joint prior to implanting 
the tissue results in the differentiation of the cartilage cells to the optimum articular cartilage. 
This is further evidenced by the evaluation of articular hyaline cartilage biomarkers prior to 
release of the implant. Patients treated with NeoCart demonstrated a statistically significant 
faster recovery at 6 months post index procedure that is durable and continues to improve 
through up to the two years for which data is available. 
In summary, based on our review of publicly available information regarding current standards, 
we believe the NeoCart Phase III study meets the FDA’s current guidance in terms of conduct, 
patient demographics and inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the pain and function endpoints as 
chosen are appropriate to demonstrate efficacy and safety of an investigational treatment for 
knee cartilage injury. 
13.2. 
Overall conclusion 
In conclusion, NeoCart’s clinical effectiveness was demonstrated through clinically meaningful 
and statistically significant treatment related improvements in pain and function at the 1-year 
timepoint versus the microfracture control arm. The data become even more powerful as lesion 
size increases above the 2.0cm2 size.  While the limited application of Microfracture in larger 
lesions has been recognized this is the first study to clearly define the lesion size above which the 
risk of even intermediate term (1-year) may be too great for physicians and patients to accept.  
NeoCart offers a durable and safe option.  The NeoCart phase 3 clinical study results 
demonstrate clinical benefit with a very acceptable risk profile. The ability to get patients back 
on their feet in half the time has demonstrable advantages from a health economics perspective, 
particularly in a broad range of lesions where microfracture is most often used, not in limited 
populations where it is no longer used. 
These data were generated from the largest adequate and well-controlled Phase III clinical study 
to date in a U.S representative patient population with stringent inclusion/exclusion standards 
based on FDA’s input. The efficacy of NeoCart was measured using validated and FDAaccepted 
instruments such as KOOS pain and IKDC function that that can be directly correlated to 
clinically relevant benefits for patients.

14.3.3. 
Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events 
Patient 03-002 (NeoCart): 
Event 1: Patient experienced Arthralgia that was first reported January 1, 2011, approximately 5 
months after implantation on August 13, 2010.The patient was diagnosed with Chondral 
Degeneration (MedDra Cartilage Atrophy) at arthroscopy on October 12, 2012, at which time 
chondroplasty of a flap tear adjacent to the NeoCart implant, as well as approximately 50% of 
the NeoCart implant, was performed.  Following the procedure, the patient reported immediate 
relief of pain.  The Investigator assessed the event of Arthralgia as severe in severity and 
possibly related to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.   
Event 2: On December 20, 2012, the patient was hospitalized for a self-inflicted gunshot wound 
to the non-study leg.  The patient underwent an operation to fixate a fractured femur and irrigate 
and debride the wound.  The patient was discharged on December 23, 2012 in stable condition.  
The Investigator assessed the event of Gun Shot Wound as severe in severity and unrelated to 
both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.  
The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on September 18, 2013. 
Patient 03-005 (NeoCart): 
Event 1: Patient suffered a Meniscus Injury (left medial meniscus tear) in the target knee on 
August 8, 2010, after randomization/biopsy, but prior to the implantation procedure.  The
